en: During the day, land heats faster than the ocean, causing warm air to rise and cool sea air to rush inland as a breeze.
Water trapped in rock cracks freezes and expands, which pushes the rocks apart and breaks them into smaller pieces.
Earth's tilted axis causes different hemispheres to receive varying amounts of direct sunlight throughout the year, creating the four seasons.
The Moon's gravitational pull continuously tugs on Earth's oceans, causing the water levels to rise and fall as high and low tides.
An underwater earthquake suddenly displaces the ocean floor, which pushes the water above it to form massive tsunami waves.
As warm, moist air rises and cools in the atmosphere, the water vapor condenses into tiny liquid droplets that form clouds.
Magma that cools very slowly deep underground allows large mineral crystals to grow, forming coarse-grained igneous rocks like granite.
When a massive star exhausts its nuclear fuel, its core collapses under gravity and explodes outward as a supernova.
Earthworms digest decaying plant matter and excrete nutrient-rich castings, which naturally fertilize the soil and improve its structure.
Tectonic plates stuck together suddenly slip and release stored elastic energy, sending seismic waves through the ground that cause earthquakes.
Warm ocean water evaporates and rises, releasing heat energy that powers the spinning winds of a tropical cyclone or typhoon.
Slightly acidic rainwater dissolves limestone bedrock over thousands of years, carving out underground caverns and forming stalactites.
